Reference.Title: Unmasking the Mystery
Reference.Address: [Botrous, Fady; Seby, Robert; Fricker-Sauls, Rachel; Mansour, Megan; Wilson, Claire; Hill, Ebone] Mayo Clin Florida, 4500 Sab Pablo Rd, Jacksonville, FL 32224 USA
Reference.Abstract: While Mycoplasma pneumoniae (MP) is a well-known cause of walking pneumonia, it has been documented to cause more severe complications, including extrapulmonary manifestations. This is a case of a 41-year-old male patient with recurrent pneumonia, necrotizing pneumonitis, and bilateral panuveitis caused by persistent MP infection despite previous completion of broad spectrum antibiotic treatment, including ampicillin/sulbactam, amoxicillin/clavulanate, and doxycycline. He was treated with 500 mg/day of azithromycin for 7 days. He received intravenous pulse dose methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 3 days, followed by oral prednisone at 60 mg daily, which was tapered down over several weeks. He was also treated with cyclopentolate 1% solution eye drops 3 times daily, timolol 0.5% solution eye drops twice daily, and prednisolone 1% solution eye drops every hour. The mechanism of these manifestations is unclear, although it is likely due to a systemic proinflammatory cascade that results in severe pulmonary infection and extrapulmonary manifestations. These manifestations can make the diagnosis obscure and difficult to reach without a strong clinical workup and a high degree of suspicion. The incidence of necrotizing pneumonitis and uveitis caused by MP is relatively low (0.5%-2%) and the incidence of uveitis caused by MP is likely even lower. Furthermore, these manifestations have never previously been documented in the same patient. Although rare, necrotizing pneumonitis caused by MP infection is associated with prolonged hospital stays, increased requirement for mechanical ventilatory support, increased pleural and cardiac complications, as well as a high in-hospital mortality rate of 29.4% for those who require intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Therefore, it is important to have this suspicion as early management with steroids and antibiotic therapy may be key to halting the proinflammatory response.
